notes: Considered the first practical, automobile and the first to be put into series production
The Flocken Elektrowagen, designed by German entrepreneur and inventor Andreas Flocken, is regarded as the first electric production car
Considered the first modern car, and a significant advancement over the previous generation of modified stagecoach automobiles.
Named 'The Silver Ghost' by virtue of its appearance and "extraordinary stealthiness", Autocar magazine called this "The Best Car in the World" in 1907
Transformed global manufacturing with the introduction of the world’s first moving assembly line for mass automotive production. Over almost 20 years, Ford produced some 15 million models.
This 21.5 litre, 'bird-beaked' vehicle set a land speed record of 141 mph, said to be "faster than any plane, train, or automobile" at the time.
The first vehicle produced by A.L.F.A., featuring advanced multi-valve head engineering and immediate racing success.
The first true 'Bugatti', built in German Alsace before the region became part of France. The car pioneered multivalve engines and was a racing success.
Widely regarded as Britain’s first purpose-built sports car, designed for high-speed endurance trials.
Citroën's inaugural vehicle and Europe's first mass-produced car built using mass production assembly line principles.
The Rumpler Tropfenwagen ("Rumpler drop car", named after its raindrop shape) was developed to be streamlined with a very low drag coefficient.
Britain's answer to the Ford Model T, an economic, mass-produced car, licensed and adapted across Europe, the US and Japan.
World’s first production car to feature a load-bearing monocoque chassis and independent front suspension.
A phenomenally successful racing car, winning over 1,000 races and pioneering the concept of a holistically conceived, race-ready car available for purchase
The first Chrysler car, technically advanced and an affordable price point.
Iconic endurance sports car that defined British racing pedigree.
Successfully replaced the Model T by introducing modern driver controls, standard safety glass, and contemporary styling.
The pinnacle of pre-war American luxury and power, featuring a DOHC 32-valve straight-eight engine capable of 116 mph.
Designed by Ferdinand Porsche, this supercharged performance car dominated hillclimbs and Grand Prix events worldwide.
Vittorio Jano-designed sports racer that dominated pre-war sports car racing, including multiple Mille Miglia victories.
The outrageous remodelling of the already luxury Cadillac V-16, ordered by by Philippe Barraud, a wealthy playboy of the 1930s, who wanted a bespoke automobile to suit his lavish lifestyle.
Dominant pre-war sports racer featuring a supercharged straight-eight engine and four consecutive Le Mans victories.
One of the first cars designed with aerodynamics in mind, in order to reduce airflow
Translating literally to 'Front-wheel drive', the Traction Avant pioneered the mass-production front-wheel drive cars.
The longest continuous vehicle nameplate in history, evolving across 12 generations from a truck-based station wagon into a full-size SUV.
The original Fiat 500, Topolino is Italian for 'little mouse', and this was one of the smallest cars in the world at the time of its production
Iconic pre-war sports car that was the first to wear the 'Jaguar' name, establishing Sir William Lyons' philosophy of elegance and performance.
The pinnacle of pre-war German luxury grand touring, featuring a supercharged straight-eight engine and bespoke coachwork.
World’s first production car equipped with an electrically powered retractable hardtop roof.
Pinnacle of pre-war grand touring engineering, combining a twin-supercharged straight-eight engine with advanced independent suspension.
Dominant Grand Prix car that secured victory in the inaugural Formula 1 World Championship race and back-to-back world titles.
Widely acknowledged as the automotive industry's first concept car, introducing concealed headlights and flush door handles.
Commissioned by Adolf Hitler as an affordable "people's car", this became one of the most produced vehicles in history.
Iconic luxury wagon line famed for its genuine ash and mahogany wood body framing in the 1940s before evolving into a premium full-size estate.
Standardised light four-wheel-drive military vehicle that established the blueprint for all modern off-road vehicles.
Adapted directly from WWII military vehicles, serving as North America's first mass-produced 4x4 civilian pickup.
Defined post-war American automotive luxury and introduced iconic styling cues like VentiPorts and the Riviera hardtop
The first vehicle produced by Ferrari, powered by Gioachino Colombo's 1.5-litre V12 engine and establishing the brand's racing origins.
A masterclass in utilitarian genius originally designed to carry a farmer and a basket of eggs across a ploughed field without breaking them, ultimately evolving into an enduring bohemian icon.

An upscale alternative to the Standard Ford model. It was transformed into "Greased Lightnin'" in the movie Grease, given by Mr Miyagi to Daniel in the Karate Kid, and was Biff Tannen's manure-filled car in Back to the Future
Australia’s first mass-produced car, establishing the domestic automotive manufacturing industry.
Introduced the legendary XK twin-cam engine and debuted as the fastest production car in the world.

Inspired by the US Willys Jeep, thie Land Rover defined British civilian four-wheel-drive capability for decades, with Land Rover claiming in 1992 that 70% of all the vehicles they had built were still in use.
The utility vehicle that birthed the brand, built with an aluminium-manganese alloy body on a box-section chassis; became an international symbol of rugged durability and exploration.
Alec Issigonis-designed family car that democratised post-war British motoring and became the first British vehicle to exceed one million sales.
The first production model to bear the Porsche name, establishing the brand's lightweight, rear-engine sports car identity.
Oldsmobile's most popular line from 1950 to 1974, pairing a lightweight body with the high-compression Rocket V8 engine, establishing the blueprint for the American muscle car.
Saab's first production car. The iconic Saab green was due to Saab aquiring large quantities of a green cellulose paint that was sold off by the armed forces having proved unsuitable for camouflage.
Alfa Romeo’s first left-hand-drive car and first unitary chassis, marking the company's transition to mass assembly line manufacturing.
The car that launched Juan Manuel Fangio onto the Formula 1 stage, winning his very first World Championship in 1951 driving the evolution 159 variant.

The iconic choice of surfers worldwide, the second generation T2 cemented the 'VW Camper' lifestyle. Volkswagen partnered heavily with coachbuilders like Westfalia to factory-offer pop-up camper roofs, folding beds, and integrated kitchenets
Purpose-built sports racer that secured Jaguar's first overall victories at Le Mans (1951, 1953) and pioneered disc brakes in motorsport.
Aerodynamic Mulliner-bodied fastback coupe regarded as one of the most elegant and fastest four-seat sports tourers of its era.
America's longest unbroken sports car production run, this is the original Chevrolet Corvette, that began a massive 70+ year history spanning eight distinct generations.

The iconic Ford F-series, one of the longest-running car brands of all time, in continuous production since 1948. Instantly recognisable from its rounded shape, the 2nd generation model is an absolute icon of American hot-rod culture and arguably the most modified classic truck of all time.
Iconic egg-shaped bubble car featuring a front-opening refrigerator door, originally designed by Iso in Italy and built under licence by BMW.

url: An avant-garde masterpiece, first introduced in 1955. The DS is defined by its revolutionary hydropneumatic self-levelling suspension, directional headlights, and futuristic aerodynamics.
notes: An elegant alternative to mainstream hatchbacks, blending emotive Italian design with punchy turbo performance and agile road manners
Aeronautically inspired monocoque racer featuring a iconic rear tail fin, dominating the 24 Hours of Le Mans with three consecutive wins (1955–1957).

Widely considered the most beautiful and perfectly balanced Grand Prix car ever made, the 250F is forever tied to the 1957 German Grand Prix at the Nürburgring, in which Juan Manuel Fangio recovered from a botched pit-stop by breaking the track lap record ten times in a row, winning the race on the final lap and securing the F1 title.
The iconic Mercedes 300 SL, with it's 'gullwing' doors - introduced in 1954 as a road-going version of the W194 racing car, the marque has remained in continuous production to the present day.
Built and  tailored specifically for Juan Manual Fangio, he used it to dominate and capture back-to-back F1 World Championships in 1954 and 1955

An avant-garde masterpiece defined by revolutionary hydropneumatic self-levelling suspension, directional headlights, and futuristic aerodynamics that stunned the world upon its 1955 Paris Motor Show debut.
Two-seat personal luxury car created to counter the Chevrolet Corvette, blending sporty styling with grand touring comfort.
Aircraft-inspired tandem two-seater Kabinenroller (cabin scooter) with a transparent acrylic bubble canopy and handlebar steering.
A breathtaking collaboration marrying Carrozzeria Ghia's Italian flair with rugged Volkswagen Beetle mechanicals, creating an affordable design masterpiece that defined post-war optimism.
Legendary sports racing car that achieved overall victory at the 1959 24 Hours of Le Mans and the World Sportscar Championship.
Exquisite Albrecht von Goertz-designed V8 roadster; despite heavy financial losses per unit, it became an enduring design icon owned by Elvis Presley.
Rugged executive saloon built to withstand harsh climate conditions, serving as the primary Soviet official and taxi vehicle.
Massively popular rear-engine family car that expanded Renault's international presence, selling over two million units worldwide.
Distinctive aerodynamic rear-engined V8 luxury car reserved exclusively for high-ranking party officials and foreign dignitaries.
Iconic family car that became the first vehicle in the world to feature three-point seatbelts as standard equipment.
Dominant sports racing car featuring distinctive 'pontoon fender' bodywork, securing multiple 24 Hours of Le Mans victories.
A genius exercise in minimalist packaging that motorized post-war Italy with a lovable, rear-engined canvas-top runabout.
Unique Australian-designed fibreglass micro-sports car built on an imported German chassis, made famous in a 1990s Yellow Pages TV advert.
Lightweight fibreglass sports car developed by Glass Sport Motors that achieved notable racing success in Europe and Africa.
Based on the Morris Oxford III, this iconic "King of Indian Roads" served politicians and public transport fleets for over five decades.
Recognized as South Africa’s first commercially built production car, featuring a fibreglass body on a tubular frame.
Affordable, lightweight sports car built using Austin mechanicals, famous for its distinct bug-eyed headlamp styling and accessible fun.

In 1958 Fiat shipped a number of Fiat 600s to the Italian design house Ghia for conversion into a beach car. Featuring wicker seats and the option of a fringed top to shield its occupants from the Mediterranean sun, these cars were originally made for use on large yachts of the wealthy (Aristotle Onassis owned one)
China’s first official state limousine, built specifically for government ceremonies and high-ranking political leadership.
The iconic two-door, four-seat small car produced for four decades over a single generation, with over 5 million models made and countless variant and customisations.
Introduced the newly developed all-aluminium 6.25-litre L-series V8 engine, setting the mechanical benchmark for decades.
Showcased the absolute peak of 1950s tailfin design before evolving into Cadillac's core luxury saloon line.
The ultimate rolling sculpture of American postwar optimism and excess, defined by its towering, razor-sharp tailfins and dual bullet taillights.
Miller-Meteor produced professional vehicles such as ambulances and hearses. The iconic 'Ectomobile' was a modified 1959 Cadillac / Miller-Meteor ambulance for the 1984 film, Ghostbusters.
The 1959, 6th generation Cadillac 62 is remembered for its iconic huge tailfins with dual bullet tail lights.
Definitive luxury sports saloon combining a compact bodyshell with potent XK straight-six engines, becoming a British culture icon.
Licence-built derivative of the BMC Farina / Riley 4 saloon that became the quintessential mid-century Argentine taxi icon.
Fitted with a sailboat mast and keel by James May for the Top Gear amphibious car challenge, successfully sailing across Reservoir waters before capsizing near the shore.

A cornerstone of American automotive history, transitioning from a quirky late-fifties full-size car into one of the most rugged, ubiquitous compacts ever built, later spawning famous compact muscle variants like the GTS and Demon.
Pininfarina-styled family saloon globally celebrated for extraordinary reliability and mechanical durability, selling nearly 3 million units.
Aerodynamic, rally-winning compact car that established Saab’s international reputation for durability and engineering.
The definitive Alpine model, spanning two distinct eras: the legendary 1960s/70s rally champion and the highly acclaimed modern mid-engined sports car revived in 2017
Introduced in 1961, the original Mini Cooper S dominated the 1960s rally scene with its light weight and corner-carving ability.
Distinctive family car famous for its reverse-rake rear window styling, becoming the best-selling car in France in 1966.
Immortalised as the ultimate symbol of automotive desire and teenage rebellion in Ferris Bueller’s Day Off.
Malcolm Sayer-designed masterpiece blending 150 mph performance, race-derived aerodynamics, and revolutionary value; Enzo Ferrari called it the most beautiful car ever made.
The definitive post-war British sports car; over half a million MGBs were built, making it an accessible, wind-in-the-hair global icon.
First introduced in 1961, Renault's first front-wheel-drive family hatchback, featuring a flat load floor and versatile tailgate; sold over 8 million units globally.
Sleek sports coupe famous for its TV appearance in The Saint and for setting the highest certified vehicle mileage record.
Saved BMW from financial ruin and created the modern compact sports saloon segment, introducing the signature 'Hofmeister kink'.
Lotus revolutionised F1 by making lighter, tighter, sleeker cars. Jim Clark weaponised the Lotus 25, taking 14 Grand Prix victories and capturing the 1963 F1 World Championship in dominant fashion
Groundbreaking roadster featuring a steel backbone chassis, fibreglass body, and twin-cam engine; inspired the Mazda MX-5.
Isle of Man-built single-seater holding the Guinness World Record as the smallest production car ever made; fitted with a rear handle for maneuvering instead of a reverse gear.
Iconic hybrid created by mating a small-block Ford V8 to the lightweight Ace chassis, dominating 1960s sports car racing.
First produced in 1963, the DB5 became widely known after being used by James Bond in the 1964 film Goldfinger (although author Ian Fleming had placed Bond in a DB Mark III in the novel).
Landmark personal luxury coupe designed by Ned Nickles, acclaimed for its razor-edge styling and high performance.
Experimental Ghia-bodied coupe powered by a gas turbine engine capable of running on multiple fuels, distributed to the public in a nationwide user trial.
Honda's inaugural passenger sports cars featuring high-revving engines, chain-drive rear axles (in early models), and sports styling.
Ultra-luxury limousine engineered without financial restraint, featuring complex high-pressure hydraulics favoured by world leaders and royalty.
First introduced in 1964, the 911 has remained both a sporting and style icon throughout the eight distinct generations of its 60-plus year production run.
Massively successful light family car produced across three generations, providing affordable motoring for post-war Britain.

This 1963 VW Beetle is quite possibly the most famous version of the most famous car of all time. Herbie, the 'Love Bug', is a fictional sentient 1963 Volkswagen Beetle racing car that was featured in several Walt Disney motion pictures.
American-financed endurance race car built to defeat Ferrari, securing four consecutive overall wins at Le Mans (1966–1969).
Created the 'pony car' market segment, combining long-hood and short-deck styling with affordable performance and vast options.
The original glass-fibre dune buggy built on a shortened VW Beetle floorpan, sparking a global kit-car phenomenon.
The ultimate 'beach buggy' - the stripped-back, doorless Mini Moke failed as a lightweight army vehicle but found global fame as a chic, sun-soaked coastal icon.
Licence-built derivative of the Fiat 1100 Delight that became the quintessential Mumbai taxi and a symbol of mid-century urban transport.
Served as the primary government official and taxi fleet passenger car across China for nearly three decades.
Skoda's economic alternative to the western rear-engined family cars like the Renault 8 or VW Beetle.
Duroplast-bodied "people's car" that became an enduring cultural icon of East German motoring.
Combined elegant Pietro Frua Italian coachwork with a 7.0-litre Ford V8 built upon an extended Cobra Mk III chassis.
Lightweight, aluminium-panelled homologation special that achieved dominant success in touring car racing worldwide.

Custom-built sports estate created by Harold Radford for company owner David Brown. In August 2019 a DB5 Shooting Brake sold for a record $1.765m (£1.456m), aking it the most valuable Shooting Brake-bodied car of any marque sold at auction.
Shifting the engine up front like a car, the landmark 1965 First-Generation (Mk1) Ford Transit completely revolutionized commercial vans with its car-like handling and wide, highly versatile track
Massively popular mid-size series that became the single best-selling car model in North America during the late 1970s and 1980s.
The first Rolls-Royce with a monocoque chassis, featuring advanced high-pressure hydraulic self-levelling suspension and all-round disc brakes.
The quintessential American muscle car, reimagined by Shelby for the race track, with its iconic dual front to back distinctive stipes.
Iconic Pininfarina-designed roadster that remained in production across four distinct generations over nearly three decades.
Engineered under the code name 'G.O.A.T. - Goes Over Any Type of Terrain - the 1966 Ford Bronco paired rugged four-wheel drive with highly customizable utility.
Celebrated Argentine performance icon that adapted American underpinnings with Pininfarina styling and local engine engineering.

A swaggering, ultra-stylish grand tourer wrapped in Carrozzeria Touring sheet metal and propelled by a roaring Chrysler V8, perfectly capturing the bold, swaggering spirit of 1960s and 70s luxury motoring.
Pioneering transverse mid-engine V12 layout styled by Marcello Gandini at Bertone, widely acknowledged as the world's first true supercar.
The Lincoln Future concept car was displayed on the auto show circuit in 1955, before being customised by George Barris in 1966 for the TV show, Batman.
Landmark front-wheel-drive personal luxury coupe featuring radical styling and a unitised transaxle layout.
Ultra-exclusive road-going derivative of the Tipo 33 racer featuring butterfly doors and an ultra-high-revving mid-mounted V8.
Best-selling family car that established Ford's motorsport dominance in international rallying, particularly in Twin-Cam and RS1600 guises.

The Lotus 49 pioneered two massive structural design milestones: the fully integrated stressed-member engine and the dawn of aerodynamic wings. It won on its debut in 1967 with Jim Clark, carried Graham Hill to the 1968 title, and secured Lotus the 1968 and 1970 Constructors' Championships
Mazda's halo sports car that successfully introduced the world's first dual-rotor Wankel rotary engine to volume production.
License-built modification of the Fiat 124/125 that formed the backbone of Polish post-war passenger transport.
Limited-production front-mid-engine sports coupe co-developed with Yamaha that proved Japan could build world-class sports cars.
Unbroken manufacturing run spanning seven generations, evolving from the original air-cooled T1 split-screen to modern passenger and commercial variants.
Debuted as a limited-production luxury convertible, the Skylark underwent one of the most dramatic evolutions in American automotive history, transforming into a formidable muscle icon
Brazil’s quintessential muscle car, featuring bold rally stripes and a high-torque 4.1-litre inline-six engine based on an Opel platform.

The heavyweight champion of the muscle car wars, the second generation, 1970 Chevelle SS paired an aggressively redesigned, bulking body with the legendary V8 to unleash the highest factory horsepower rating of its entire era
America's longest unbroken sports car production run, the Chevrolet Corvette has a massive 70+ year history spanning eight distinct generations.
The Citroën Méhari was a lightweight, plastic-bodied utility car built on a 2CV chassis that became a beloved French lifestyle icon and a rugged seaside favorite
A muscular, Pininfarina-penned front-engine V12 icon that defined 1970s supercar culture and famously swept its class at the 24 Hours of Le Mans.

The 1968 Ford Mustang GT Fastback is one of cinema's most famous cars. It is celebrated for starring in a nearly 10-minute, dialogue-free car chase through the streets of San Francisco as Lieutenant Frank Bullitt pursues hitmen in a Dodge Charger
The Holden Monaro GTS 327 was Holden's first sports coupe, won the brand's first Bathurst 500 victory, and ignited the legendary "Ford vs. Holden" racetrack war.
Iconic British roadster combining classic coachbuilt aesthetics with thumping Rover and later BMW V8 performance.
1969 European Car of the Year with independent rear suspension; affectionately known as 'Africa's workhorse' for its incredible ruggedness.
Credited with popularising the 1960s American muscle car. The second generation of the GTO, came with a wild, spoiler-clad performance option in 'The Judge'
A cult icon that popularised the two-door sports estate concept for the mass market.
World's first British five-door hatchback featuring a transverse engine, five-speed transmission, and seats that folded completely flat into a bed.
General Motors UK's direct challenger to the Ford Transit, the Bedford CF was a ubiquitous sight throughout the 70s and 80s, used for everything from campervans to police riot vans to ice cream vans
Invented to outsmart British tax laws, the 1957 Bedford CA Dormobile pioneered the modern campervan with its iconic candy-striped side-pop roof
License-built variant of the Renault 12 that served as Romania’s primary national family car for over three decades.

The iconic orange 1969 Dodge Charger driven in the television series The Dukes of Hazzard. It is known for its signature horn, long jumps, and for having its doors welded shut, requiring the Dukes to climb in and out through the windows.
Mid-engine V6 sports car named after Enzo Ferrari's late son, laying the architectural foundation for Ferrari's core mid-engine road cars.
Revolutionary sports car that combined sleek styling, independent suspension, and a smooth straight-six engine at an accessible price point worldwide.
Targa-topped mid-engine entry-level sports car developed jointly with Volkswagen, offering balanced handling and dual boot space.
The 1969 3/30 incarnation of the Reliant Supervan, immortalised as Del Boy's beaten up three-wheel van in the British sitcom, Only Fools and Horses

Celebrated as Australia’s greatest premier home-grown V8 sports car, pairing a lightweight fibreglass body with Ford V8 power. Unlike the mainstream heavy-iron muscle cars from Ford and Holden, the Nagari was a sleek, lightweight fiberglass boutique sports car designed to take on European marques like Lotus and TVR.
Wedge-shaped, three-wheeled micro-coupé featuring a lift-up canopy, vibrant orange paintwork, and Reliant four-cylinder mechanicals.
American muscle car royalty, first launched in 1967 and since locked in a decades-long horsepower war with the Ford Mustang.
High-performance luxury grand tourer pairing Citroën's hydropneumatic tech and DIRAVI speed-sensitive steering with a Maserati quad-cam V6 engine.
A massive commercial success the Ford Cortina was first introduced in 1962 and was Britain's best-selling car for nine out of ten years between 1972 and 1981.
The Lotus 72 looked like a spaceship compared to anything else on the grid, establishing the visual silhouette that modern Formula 1 cars still use today.
Japanese fastback coupe heavily influenced by American muscle styling, featuring a rear ducktail spoiler and dual-overhead-cam engine options.
The Plymouth Superbird paired a towering rear wing and a massive nose cone with a roaring Hemi V8 to shatter stock-car speed records
Pioneered the luxury SUV market by combining permanent four-wheel drive and long-travel coil spring suspension with a plush, comfortable cabin.
Distinctive luxury 2+2 grand tourer featuring a built-in roll-over safety bar, Michelotti styling, and an ambitious, custom-designed 3.0-litre V8 engine.
A massive luxury cruiser packing a monstrous 500-cubic-inch V8 engine, famously marketed by GM as "the last American convertible"
Peak of early Australian muscle, famously claiming the title of the world’s fastest production four-door sedan upon release.
Traditional rear-wheel-drive family car and fleet staple that achieved massive commercial sales success in 1970s Britain. Immortalised as a running joke on the Top Geat TV series
Groundbreaking front-wheel-drive compact hatchback praised for its boxer engine layout and exceptional dynamic handling.
Iconic short-wheelbase muscle car featuring a potent 265 cu in "Hemi" straight-six with triple Weber carburettors.
Game-changing hatchback that put Honda on the global automotive map, featuring the innovative CVCC engine that met strict US emissions standards without a catalytic converter.
The definitive standard of executive luxury, safety, and over-engineering.
Charming, lightweight supermini featuring wrapped polyester bumpers; redefined urban transport and became France's best-selling car for a decade.

Striking sports coupe - described by a German technology magazine as the "most beautiful Volkswagen in the world" - the SP2 (named after Sao Paolo) was designed entirely in Brazil to circumvent strict national restrictions on foreign imports.

The iconic variant of the classic Swedish sports car that features a two-door shooting brake (sports estate) layout. Introduced late in the car's production cycle, it remains one of the most distinctive and influential automotive designs in history
Europe's first turbocharged production car, delivering explosive performance and establishing BMW's forced-induction credentials.
Buick's entry into the personal luxury market that combined formal styling, opera windows, and plush interiors to capture the upscale buyers of the 1970s.
Direct evolution of the Lotus Seven design, first introduced in 1973 and famed for uncompromising raw speed, pure analog feedback, and phenomenal power-to-weight ratios.
Longest-running generation of GM's full-size truck platform, defining 1970s and 1980s utility and immortalised in the 80s TV show, The Fall Guy

The iconic Ford F-series, one of the longest-running car brands of all time, in continuous production since 1948. The 6th generatrion was America’s best-selling truck in 1977, a title it has held ever since
The world's first purpose-built rally supercar, winning three consecutive WRC manufacturers' titles in 1974, 1975 and 1976 in the hands of Sandro Munari and Björn Waldegård
The Puma GTB (Gran Turismo Brazil) is a front-engine, rear-wheel-drive sports coupe that was Brazil's most expensive and prestigious luxury car for over a decade.
Indigenously designed Brazilian hatchback-estate hybrid that achieved massive commercial success across Latin America.
1975 European Car of the Year named for its exceptionally low drag coefficient; served as the brand's luxury flagship for nearly two decades.
The iconinc Blues Brothers' Bluesmobile; a decommissioned Mount Prospect police car, purchased by Elwood Blues at an auction after he had traded a previous car for a microphone.
The iconic muscle car used by 'Mad' Max Rockatansky to exact his revenge on an outlaw motorcycle gang who killed his wife and son in the 1979 film, Mad Max
The 1974, third generation Torino defined 70s television cop culture with its distinctive "striped tomato" paint scheme in Starsky & Hutch.
Charming, quintessential British sports car icon that brought stylish, affordable open-top motoring to the masses.
The definitive 'hot hatch' delivering sports car performance in an everyday practical run-around.
Sleek front-wheel-drive sports coupe designed by Giorgetto Giugiaro, introduced alongside the Golf as a modern replacement for the Karmann Ghia.

One of the most durable, utilitarian vehicles ever manufactured. Produced by Volvo from 1974 until 1993, this legendary 'box' became a global symbol of family practicality, automotive safety, and understated style thorughout the 1980s.

The birth of the 'ultimate driving machine', the BMW 3 Series invented the modern executive sports sedan, defining BMW's driver-focused DNA with its iconic shark-nose styling. The marque has remained in continuous production for over 50 years through seven generations.
Chrysler's hugely successful entry into the 1970s personal luxury coupe market, famous for its distinctive styling and 'Corinthian leather' interior options.
One of the most successful rally cars of all time. The Ford works team was practically unbeatable in the late 1960s and early 1970s.
Distinctive grand tourer with flying buttress styling, powered by Jaguar's smooth 5.3-litre V12 engine across a 21-year production run.

The Porsche 930 was a turbocharged variant of the 911 manufactured between 1975 and 1989. The definitive sports car of the 1980s, it was the top-of-the-range 911 model for its entire production duration and, at the time of its introduction, was the fastest production car in Germany
Radical 'wedge' shaped sports car ('the shape of things to come'); the rare TR8 variant shoehorned the Rover V8 into the chassis to create a potent British muscle car.
Compact hatchback staple that spawned the high-performance 2.3-litre HS and HSR rally homologation specials, conquering British rallying.
Legendary fleet and family car series that defined British roads for two decades, fiercely competing with the Ford Cortina and Sierra.
Compact supermini rebadged from the Audi 50, expanding Volkswagen's water-cooled front-wheel-drive range into smaller vehicle classes.

The 1976 'Mirthmobile' driven by Wayne Campbell and Garth Algar in the 1990s films Wayne's World I and II. The car featured prominently in the films, most notably during the headbanging sing-along to Queen's 'Bohemian Rhapsody'.
Radical wedge-shaped luxury saloon designed by William Towns, pioneering digital LED and CRT dashboard instrumentation.
Adapted Fiat 127 derivative that pioneered the world’s first mass-produced ethanol-fuelled production engine in 1979.
Larger hatchback and saloon that established Honda's reputation for building reliable, fuel-efficient family cars internationally.
Striking, Pininfarina-inspired five-door executive hatchback powered by the Rover V8, serving as a prominent police pursuit vehicle and successful touring car racer.

Widely dubbed Britain’s first supercar, featuring aggressive muscular styling, a blanked-off grille, and a 375 bhp 5.3-litre V8. The car was immortalised in the 1987 James Bond film, The Living Daylights
The Lada Niva has been in continuous production since 1977 and pioneered the modern compact crossover layout by offering permanent four-wheel drive to rural, urban and family users.
Known as the 'Wet Nellie' and famous for its transformation into a fully functional submarine in the 1977 James Bond film, The Spy Who Loved Me.
The iconic car in which Bo "Bandit" Darville gives Sheriff Buford T. Justice the runaround in the film, Smokey and the Bandit
Front-engine V8 grand tourer featuring the Weissach rear axle; remains the only sports car to win European Car of the Year (1978).
BMW's first mid-engine supercar and the inaugural standalone vehicle developed by BMW Motorsport GmbH, styled by Giorgetto Giugiaro.
High-performance muscle truck in a colour scheme intended to match a Palomino horse
Marketed as Europe’s answer to the Mustang, the third generation Ford Capri became a major British cultural icon, achieving TV fame in the 80s cop show, The Professionals
Hatchback family car engineered with over one million units produced and remaining a Polish staple for decades.

The iconic black and gold livery on the Lotus 79, a car which introduced 'Ground Effect' aerodynamics that created a vacuum literally sucking the car onto the track. The Lotus 79 was so vastly superior to the rest of the field in 1978 that Mario Andretti easily cruised to the World Championship, securing Lotus its final Constructors' title.
An extreme, long-tailed aerodynamic masterpiece built for the Mulsanne straight, famously nicknamed after the white whale and packing a fire-breathing twin-turbocharged flat-six.
The Saab 99 Turbo was one of the first 'family cars' to be fitted with a turbo, moving the technology from low-volume sports cars to the mass-market.
The 308 was made famous by the television series Magnum, P.I. in which the series' lead, Thomas Magnum drove the car around Oahu while on his investigations, from 1980 to 1988
The iconic black Lamborghini driven by racer J.J. McClure and his buddy, Victor Prinzim (aka 'Captain Chaos') in the 1981 film, The Cannonball Run
Vauxhall's cornerstone hatch, one of the most defining and ubiquitous family car nameplates in British automotive history, locked in a decades-long sales battle for the nation's heartland.
Critically important supermini that revived British Leyland's fortunes, praised for clever packaging and fuel efficiency.
Named after the legendary Le Mans straight, it marked Bentley's vital modern renaissance after decades in the shadow of Rolls-Royce
An iconic, art-deco-inspired two-tone masterpiece that became the chic, high-spirited swan-song symbol of the eccentric French classic.
Three-time WRC Manufacturers' Champion that proved a family saloon could be turned into a rally giant-killer.
A pioneer of the 'hot hatch' era, the XR2 hot hatch became a cult car beloved of boy racers throughout the 1980s.
The Yugo was derived from the Fiat 127 and became Yugoslavia's most famous international automotive export.
Unique Mexican hatchback-saloon hybrid developed locally by Vehículos Automotores Mexicanos using AMC components.
Aerodynamic landmark , featuring flush glazing that set new industry standards for efficiency.
Elevated an obscure, commercially failed 1982 sports car from Northern Ireland into a pop culture legend - the time machine used throughout the 1980s Back to the Future film trilogy.
